questions.q: How old was Aryabhata when he wrote the Aryabhatiya, and in what year?
questions.do: Press Golden age, 500–1150 and read the first story.
questions.a: He says he was 23, and the book is dated to 499 CE.

questions.q: Aryabhata's day (one turn of the Earth) was 23 h 56 m 4.1 s. How far off was he?
questions.do: Look at How close did they get?
questions.a: Today's value is 23 h 56 m 4.09 s, so he was off by about one hundredth of a second: precise to about 1 part in 9 million.

questions.q: Which place in Kerala gave its name to a famous school of mathematics and astronomy, and what did Madhava find there?
questions.a: Sangamagrama, near Irinjalakuda. Madhava wrote π and the sine as never-ending sums, about 250 years before Europeans found the same series.

questions.q: How fast does the shadow move on Jaipur's giant sundial, and how is that worked out?
questions.do: Read A stone clock you can almost watch move.
questions.a: About 1.1 mm a second. The scale is 15.15 m from the shadow's edge, and in one day the shadow goes once round a circle of that size: 2π × 15.15 m ÷ 86,400 seconds.

questions.q: Slide the year to 2000. How many space missions are lit, and which recent mission carries on Kodaikanal's work of watching the Sun?
questions.do: Move the year slider, then press Space age and step with Later ▸.
questions.a: By 2000 only the Aryabhata satellite (1975) is lit. Aditya-L1, at the L1 point since 6 January 2024, watches the Sun like Kodaikanal has since 1899.
